title: The Son as Judge and Saviour, and the Father Who Draws Us to Him
english: For another saying of the same kind is spoken by the same prophet in the person of the Master: “Who is it that goes to law with me? Let him stand against me. And who is it that goes to law with me? Let him come near to me” (Isaiah 50:8). That is: if anyone has just things to say, as one fortified by his deeds, let him be set against me, since I wish it, and let him come near with his arguments.

Some, however, read it this way: “Who is it that goes to law with me? Let him stand over against”—that is, facing me and somewhere far off—“me,” as one who has no good provisions for the road, and is therefore unworthy to be compared with me and to touch the most pure judgment seat. For no one begrudges the worthy if they obtain good things; these have been prepared for them.
That the Son of God is “judge of the living and the dead,” granting forgiveness of sins, and that “there is salvation in no one else.”

For he himself is “the judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42), that is, of the righteous and of sinners. He grants forgiveness of sins to those who believe in his name, and saves us by his own glory and gift. And “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12), since he is by nature merciful and Saviour, in nothing inferior to the merciful and saving God and Father. So the other Scriptures declare, and Micah in particular, saying: “Who is a God like you, taking away iniquities and passing over wrongs?” (Micah 7:18).

And Peter in the Acts, thus: “And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name” (Acts 10:42-43).

Here, then, we have him acclaimed and appointed by God because of his saving incarnation, in which he came “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). Because of it, too, it is written: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). And he is judge as one set apart from creatures; for a creature does not judge, but is subject to law and judgment.
And again: “This is the stone that was despised by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner. And there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:11-12).

He also sends a second general letter, which among other things says this too about him: “As his divine power has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and excellence, through which he has given us the greatest and precious good tidings, so that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:3-4). That is why James too said in his general letter: “There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to save and to destroy” (James 4:12).

But what need is there, after all, of a host of Scriptures for this? The Samaritans too, right-minded men, raise their voices in John, the exact spokesman of God: “For we ourselves,” they say, “have heard, and we know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, the Christ” (John 4:42); he who says gently, as Scripture says: “Take heart, child; your sins are forgiven” (Matthew 9:2).

That because the Trinity is equal in honour, the Father reveals the Son to us and draws us to him, and in turn the Son himself and the Holy Spirit bring us to the Father. Here also, on Peter’s confession, and that there is repentance.

For, so that the equal honour of the blessed Trinity in all things might be shown through everything, the Father reveals his own Son to us, draws us through himself to him, and transfers us into his kingdom (Colossians 1:13). And in turn the Son and the Holy Spirit bring us to God the Father. For God would not have transferred us to one of another substance, or greater, nor to lower powers handed down like sceptres from among his own. So the new covenant has brought the old to completion, through faith in the Son and the divine Spirit.

And they speak thus. God the Father says to the Son in Isaiah: “Behold, proselytes will come to you through me, and will dwell beside you, and will take refuge with you” (Isaiah 54:15 LXX). And the Son in John: “No one can come to me unless the heavenly Father draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:44).

And again, when Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), he replied: “Blessed are you, Peter Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it. And I will give you the keys of the heavens; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in the heavens, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in the heavens” (Matthew 16:17-19).

added_allusions.reason: “Behold, proselytes will come to you through me, and will dwell beside you, and will take refuge with you” is the Greek Isaiah 54:15 word for word; the Hebrew-based KJV verse differs, so it was checked by hand against the LXX

title: Peter’s Confession and the Unending Kingdom of the Son
english: Oh, how much faith can do, and the confession that the only-begotten God the Word is the true Son of God and not a creature!

Peter did not waver through flesh and blood when he saw God gladly dwelling on earth; that is what “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matthew 16:17) means. He recognized the branch of God that shares his nature and his eternity. In him he honoured the self-existent root without beginning that had revealed him. He believed in the oneness of Godhead that the Son has with the Father. He was declared blessed by the only blessed Master.

On this rock the churches have been built, and “the gates of Hades” (Matthew 16:18), that is, the syllogisms of heretics, shall not overcome them. He was entrusted with the keys of the heavens, so that for those who believe he might open the way in the kingdom of God, believing as Peter himself plainly answered just now, and as he heard from Christ together with the other apostles: “baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19); and that for those who do not give glory in this way he might shut the thrice-blessed and most longed-for entrance. For by the very thing for which he was called blessed, he himself was received into this glory, while those who say the opposite were rebuked and cast out.

So, having spoken the truth in confessing him the Son of God, that is, genuine and of one substance, he heard the like in return: Bar-Jonah, which is translated “son of Jonah.” And Peter was certainly not of another substance from the one who begot him.

Besides this he received authority (or rather all received it through him) not to give up on those who fall, but to receive them when they repent. For no one is without sin except the one who entrusted this authority to Peter. That is the meaning of: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in the heavens” (Matthew 18:18). From then on he cast away the inhumanity of Novatian and Sabbatius.

Paul in turn follows what has been set out, writing to the Galatians: “But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb, was pleased to reveal his Son in me” (Galatians 1:15-16); and to the Colossians: “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit for a share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (Colossians 1:12-14); and to the Corinthians: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:9); and to the Ephesians: “And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near; for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:17-18).
That the kingdom of the Only-begotten has no end.

And to put to shame the heretics who say that after the general resurrection the Son will hand over the kingdom to the Father, the Scriptures proclaim that the dominion of the Son has no end. They do so thus. Gabriel in Luke, bringing the good news to the God-bearer: “And the Lord God,” he says, “will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Israel for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32-33). And very truly so. For if he gives the kingdom back, in what kingdom of his, and when, shall we reign with him?

And Paul, writing to the Ephesians: “Every fornicator or unclean or greedy person, that is, an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Ephesians 5:5). He certainly means the kingdom after the resurrection. When, then, on their view, does he hand over the kingdom?

And to Timothy in the second letter: “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word” (2 Timothy 4:1-2). It is clear that he means the kingdom which he holds undivided and without successor with the Father and the Holy Spirit, both now and in the age to come.

And to the Hebrews: “Of the angels he says, ‘He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire’; but of the Son, ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’” (Hebrews 1:7-8). And David in the forty-fifth Psalm: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore, O God, your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (Psalm 45:6-7). See once more: his kingdom is boundless and his Godhead without beginning.

added_allusions.reason: “when shall we reign with him?” (συμβασιλεύσομεν) uses the verb of 2 Timothy 2:12, “we shall also reign with him”

title: The Son’s Unending Kingdom and the Glory Owed to Him
english: Because of his ineffable incarnation he added “your God” (Psalm 45:7). And in the hundred and forty-fifth Psalm: “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages, and your dominion is in every generation and generation” (Psalm 145:13). And in the tenth Psalm: “The Lord will reign for ever and ever” (Psalm 10:16).

And to Peter the Son, as Lord, gave the keys of the kingdom: not of the present age, for we do not yet possess it, but of the age to come, the one in which the heretics guess that he even hands it over. He gave them so that those who believe his kingdom to be without beginning and without end should be admitted, and, as was said a little earlier, those should be thrust away who do not cry out with Nathanael: “You are the Son of God, you are the King of the Christians” (John 1:49).

And the prophecy of Isaiah that says, “I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:5), Paul referred to the Spirit of God (Acts 28:25), and John, as was said before, to the Only-begotten (John 12:41), because the Godhead is shared and the one kingdom has no successor. For how could it even be that one rules and the other sits idle, as happens among men, when the Father abides in the Son and the Son in the Father (John 14:10), and when the Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26) and abides with the Son in a divine way?
On the glorifying of the Son of God himself.

So look, then, at what the saints testify once more about his glory, those “of whom,” it says, “the world was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:38). They teach us, who on earth have been called sons by grace, to glorify the only-begotten Son, who is from the substance of the Father, with a glory equal to his, and to look to the glory that he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5); for the Father does not begrudge the Beloved. The divine is free from envy and from every passion.

David, in the seventy-second Psalm, which by common consent he prophesied about Christ, says: “His name shall be blessed for ever; his name shall endure before the sun, and before the moon for generations of generations. And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all the nations shall call him blessed. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders; and blessed be the name of his glory for ever and for ever and ever. And the whole earth shall be filled with his glory. So be it” (Psalm 72:17-19).

He said “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel” in place of “glorified” or “praised.” For God is blessed by his works, that is, glorified; and he himself blesses his own creatures, that is, sanctifies them. And it should be noted that he is also God of Israel, that is, God of the fathers, just as his Father has been proclaimed.

And in the eighty-sixth Psalm, setting forth the almighty and all-powerful nature of the Only-begotten and that he ought to be glorified, he sings: “All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and shall glorify your name; for you are great and do wonders; you alone are God” (Psalm 86:9-10).

And in the nineteenth: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). How? By showing, from the greatness and beauty given them, that the one who made them, God the Word, is unsurpassable and glorified. For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6). So they are not even put to shame by the witness of lifeless things to the glory of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

And in the twenty-fourth: “Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in” (Psalm 24:7). He bids the creation below lift up the gates at his incarnation, and the creation above at his ascension. And in the hundred and seventeenth: “Praise the Lord, all you nations, and let all the peoples praise him” (Psalm 117:1).

And Isaiah: “You shall see a king with glory” (Isaiah 33:17). And Ezekiel: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place” (Ezekiel 3:12), and, “This vision is the likeness of the glory of the Lord” (Ezekiel 1:28).

Then Paul: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man” (Romans 1:22-23). And again to the Romans: “Therefore he gave them up in the desires of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonouring of their bodies among themselves. They exchanged the glory of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen” (Romans 1:24-25). And who is the maker of all, whom he says is blessed for …
